# Scope

Serialized [mlr3](https://mlr3.mlr-org.com) objects are sometimes much larger than expected.
This matters whenever an object is serialized: when it is saved with `saveRDS()`, when it is sent to a parallel worker with [future](https://cran.r-project.org/package=future), when a learner runs with encapsulation, and when [mlr3batchmark](https://mlr3batchmark.mlr-org.com) writes jobs and results to the registry.
A few extra megabytes per object can add up to gigabytes in a large benchmark experiment.
This post covers the most common causes and shows how to avoid them.
We will update it when we learn about new ones.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(mlr3)
library(mlr3pipelines)
library(mlr3tuning)
library(lobstr)
```
:::


We measure the size of an object by serializing it.
This is the number of bytes the object needs on disk or when it is sent to a parallel worker.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
serialized_size = function(x) {
  round(length(serialize(x, connection = NULL)) / 1024^2, digits = 2L)
}
```
:::


# Set the store flags

The easiest way to reduce the size of results is to store only what you need.
The functions [1:0x56bda5ef9c78] <chr> and [1:0x56bda61ebbf0] <chr> have two flags.

* `store_backends` keeps the data backend of the task in the result.
  It is `TRUE` by default.
* `store_models` keeps the trained models.
  It is `FALSE` by default.

We resample a decision tree on the spam task with 4601 emails and 57 features.
We compare the default with a call that drops the backend and a call that keeps the models.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
task = tsk("spam")
learner = lrn("classif.rpart")
resampling = rsmp("cv", folds = 3L)
resampling$instantiate(task)

rr = resample(task, learner, resampling)
rr_no_backend = resample(task, learner, resampling, store_backends = FALSE)
rr_models = resample(task, learner, resampling, store_models = TRUE)

serialized_size(rr)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2.26
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
serialized_size(rr_no_backend)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.22
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
serialized_size(rr_models)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2.53
```


:::
:::


Most of the result is the data.
Without the backend, the result is about ten times smaller.
The scores can still be computed because they only need the stored predictions.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
rr_no_backend$score(msr("classif.ce"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   task_id    learner_id resampling_id iteration classif.ce
    <char>        <char>        <char>     <int>      <num>
1:    spam classif.rpart            cv         1  0.1095176
2:    spam classif.rpart            cv         2  0.1088657
3:    spam classif.rpart            cv         3  0.1167645
Hidden columns: task, learner, resampling, prediction_test
```


:::
:::


The three decision trees add about 0.3 MB.
Models of other learners, such as a random forest, can be much larger than the data itself.
If you need the models only for prediction, the gallery post [Shrink stored models with butcher](../2026-11-05-butcher/) shows how to remove their training data.

Tuning has similar flags.
[1:0x56bd9e758cd0] <chr> stores the benchmark result of all evaluated configurations in the archive with `store_benchmark_result = TRUE` and the models with `store_models = TRUE`.
[1:0x56bd9e6dfaf8] <chr> additionally has `store_tuning_instance`.
By default, the auto tuner keeps the tuning instance and the benchmark result after training.
Both are useful to inspect the tuning process but are not needed to make predictions.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
learner_rpart = lrn("classif.rpart", cp = to_tune(1e-4, 1e-1, logscale = TRUE))

at = auto_tuner(
  tuner = tnr("random_search"),
  learner = learner_rpart,
  resampling = rsmp("cv", folds = 3L),
  term_evals = 10L
)
at$train(task)

at_lean = auto_tuner(
  tuner = tnr("random_search"),
  learner = learner_rpart,
  resampling = rsmp("cv", folds = 3L),
  term_evals = 10L,
  store_tuning_instance = FALSE,
  store_benchmark_result = FALSE
)
at_lean$train(task)

serialized_size(at)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 3.31
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
serialized_size(at_lean)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.36
```


:::
:::


The lean auto tuner is about ten times smaller.
The default auto tuner keeps the benchmark result of the 30 resampling iterations in its state, and with it the task data and all predictions.
The flags matter even more when the auto tuner runs in a nested resampling with `store_models = TRUE`, because every outer iteration then stores its own archive.

# Avoid source references

Some [mlr3](https://mlr3.mlr-org.com) objects have hyperparameters that are functions.
An example is the `applicator` of the [1:0x56bd9edadf00] <chr>, , [2:0x56bd9edadf38] <chr> pipe operator.
Learners and pipe operators keep their hyperparameters in their state after training, so these functions are serialized along with the object.

A function can carry a source reference in its `srcref` attribute.
The source reference points to an environment that holds every line of the file the function was parsed from, together with the parse data.
When the function is serialized, the whole file is serialized with it.
We simulate a source file that contains a short function followed by 10000 other lines.
We parse it once with and once without source references and evaluate the first expression, which is the function.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
code = c("function(x) x - mean(x)", rep("other_code = 1", times = 10000L))

center_srcref = eval(parse(text = code, keep.source = TRUE)[[1L]])
center = eval(parse(text = code, keep.source = FALSE)[[1L]])

serialized_size(center_srcref)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 3.59
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
serialized_size(center)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0
```


:::
:::


The function with source references needs more than 3 MB although its body is a single line.
Without source references, it needs about 100 bytes, which rounds to 0 MB.
A pipe operator that uses the function as its `applicator` inherits the problem.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
po_srcref = po("colapply", applicator = center_srcref)
po_center = po("colapply", applicator = center)

serialized_size(po_srcref)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 3.63
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
serialized_size(po_center)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.04
```


:::
:::


Functions you type into the console or source in an interactive session carry source references because the option `keep.source` is `TRUE` in interactive sessions.
The more common cause is a package installed with the `--with-keep.source` option.
Every function of such a package references the source of the complete package.
[renv](https://cran.r-project.org/package=renv) installs packages with this option by default (see [renv issue #1713](https://github.com/rstudio/renv/issues/1713)).
Since version 1.2.2, `renv` has a configuration option to disable it.
Set it before installing packages, for example in your `.Rprofile`.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
options(renv.config.install.keep.source = FALSE)
```
:::


With older versions of `renv`, set the install options of R instead.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
options(install.opts = "--without-keep.source")
```
:::


You can check whether a function carries a source reference with `attr(fun, "srcref")`.
The function `removeSource()` returns a copy of a function without it.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
serialized_size(removeSource(center_srcref))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0
```


:::
:::


# Watch the enclosing environment

A function also serializes its enclosing environment, unless it is the global environment or a package namespace.
A function created inside another function keeps all local variables of the outer function alive.
We write a helper that inspects the data of a task and returns an applicator.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
make_applicator = function(task) {
  data = task$data()
  function(x) x - mean(x)
}

applicator = make_applicator(task)
serialized_size(applicator)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 4.12
```


:::
:::


The returned function is a single line, but its environment contains the task and its data.
Every pipe operator that uses this applicator carries the complete spam data.
Create such functions in the global environment, or remove the variables you do not need from the enclosing environment before you return the function.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
make_applicator = function(task) {
  data = task$data()
  rm(data, task)
  function(x) x - mean(x)
}

applicator = make_applicator(task)
serialized_size(applicator)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0
```


:::
:::


# Duplication when serializing

In memory, R shares data between objects until one of them is modified.
This is called copy-on-write.
We create a vector `x`, assign it to `y`, and put both in a list.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
x = rnorm(1000000L)
y = x

obj_size(list(x))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
8.00 MB
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
obj_size(list(x, y))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
8.00 MB
```


:::
:::


The function `obj_size()` from [lobstr](https://cran.r-project.org/package=lobstr) accounts for shared data.
Both lists have the same size because `x` and `y` point to the same vector.
Serialization does not preserve this sharing.
Each element is written separately, and after deserializing, the two elements are independent copies.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
lxy = unserialize(serialize(list(x, y), connection = NULL))
obj_size(lxy)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
16.00 MB
```


:::
:::


The list now needs twice as much memory.
[mlr3](https://mlr3.mlr-org.com) objects often share data, for example many resample results that reference the same task.
In the session that created them, the data exists only once.
When they are sent to parallel workers or written to disk, the data is copied for each object.
[mlr3](https://mlr3.mlr-org.com) reduces the duplication in some places.
A [1:0x56bda9b8db00] <chr> stores each task, learner, and resampling only once in normalized tables.
The methods of [R6](https://cran.r-project.org/package=R6) classes are moved to the package namespace with [1:0x56bdac6aafb8] <chr>, so they are not serialized with every object.
The duplication cannot be avoided completely.

# Conclusion

Large [mlr3](https://mlr3.mlr-org.com) objects usually have one of four causes.
Results keep data or models that are not needed, functions carry source references, functions capture large enclosing environments, or shared data is duplicated during serialization.
Set the `store_*` flags to keep only what you need, install packages without source references, and check the enclosing environment of functions you pass as hyperparameters.
